doc.title: Tony Marino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 25, 2025

title: Responding in the moment: shared song forms and space
summary: Marino explains improvising through shared song forms like Autumn Leaves, listening, riffs, and leaving space on the bandstand.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Musicians, jazz players especially, talk about being in the moment. When you say respond to things, can you describe how that works to people who don’t really understand it?

Well we all know a language, a basic language. We’ve all grown up playing song forms, we’ve, you know, touched base on playing with no song form. Now song form what I mean is a definite set of rules that we play with. And we all know a lot of the same song forms. So you could be in the country like Japan and not be able to speak a word to a guy but you start playing “Autumn Leaves” and everybody knows what to do immediately. And we go off of, for instance if I think of “Autumn Leaves” I think of Miles Davis immediately. Then I think of his introduction with the G minor 6th cord, and that whole Latin thing. Or no – you know what I’m thinking, now I’m thinking of the other tune – “Blackbird.” But anyway “Autumn Leaves” I definitely think of those bands. So our ears all go to that area, you know, stuff that we’ve listened to and we can all relate by that. So on the bandstand we’re definitely choosing and picking stuff that – to get us started. So licks if you will, or riffs, you know we’ll use stuff like that when we’re improvising. The melody is another thing you know. And we’ll use the melody in improvisation too, besides the chords. But we’re listening very hard to each other. So we were trying to get somewhere that we haven’t gone before, you know a space ride if you will. So we’re listening hard and someone could make a statement, and it could be visual, it could be audible, whatever it is on the bandstand, and react to it. Or he’ll leave space. another great thing that we have on the bandstand is space. And how to use space. So a great horn player will leave space for the rhythm section to do something with it. So that’s our opportunity. Now there’s three other rhythm section members normally that are participating you know. So you’ve got to be sensitive as to when to jump and do your thing you know. But you could be a leader of, you know, this movement, or you can stand back and go for the ride you know.
